blocks.text: A single prompt rarely does all the work on its own. Real MCP servers build prompts the way good code gets built, out of small pieces that each do one job, then combined into something bigger.
Prompt composition is the practice of assembling a final prompt from parts, a system instruction, a fetched resource, a user chosen template, instead of writing one giant string by hand.
This lesson walks through why composition matters, the common patterns for combining pieces, and how to keep a composed prompt readable instead of a tangled mess.
1. What Prompt Composition Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697938-174048354.png
Composition means building a larger prompt out of smaller reusable pieces rather than writing every prompt from scratch each time.
Each piece stays independent and testable, and the composer function is the only place that knows how they fit together.
Think of it as assembly rather than authoring. Nobody writes the whole final prompt by hand, they write the parts and let a function do the joining.
2. Why Bother Composing Instead of Writing One Big Prompt
A giant hand written prompt string is fragile. Change one sentence and you risk breaking a completely different part of the behavior.
Small composable pieces can be reused across many prompts, updated once, and tested in isolation before they ever get combined.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: The same fetched resource block, the same tone instruction, the same output format rule, can all be reused across a dozen different prompt templates instead of copy pasted a dozen times.

blocks.text: A change to one shared piece then propagates everywhere it is used, instead of requiring a search and replace across a dozen separate prompt files.
3. The Three Common Building Blocks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697939-607026612.png

Most composed prompts draw from three kinds of pieces: a system instruction that sets tone and rules, resource content that supplies facts, and a user selected template that shapes the request itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Piece","Job","Where it comes from"],"rows":[["System instruction","Sets tone, constraints, and role","Fixed text the server author writes"],["Fetched resource","Supplies real, current facts","A resources/read call at request time"],["User template","Shapes what is being asked for","prompts/get with the user's chosen arguments"]]}

blocks.text: Most composition problems come down to getting the order and boundaries between these three pieces right, nothing more exotic than that.
4. Building a Prompt Out of Smaller Reusable Pieces
Think of each piece as a small function that returns a string or a message. A composer then calls these functions in order and stitches the results together.
This mirrors how good code is organized, one function per concern, one place that wires them together.
5. A Prompt That Embeds Another Prompt Output
Sometimes one prompt's job is to produce a summary, and a second prompt needs that summary as an ingredient rather than the raw source material.
The server calls prompts/get on the first prompt, takes the returned messages or the resulting text, and folds it into the second prompt's arguments.
This lets a complex workflow chain simpler prompts together instead of one prompt trying to do two jobs at once.
It also keeps each prompt focused. The summarizer only worries about summarizing well, the reply drafter only worries about tone and phrasing.
6. Combining a Template With Fetched Resource Content

blocks.alt: Combining a Template With Fetched Resource Content
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697939-997511898.png
A prompt template often has a placeholder for facts that only exist at request time, a file's current contents, a database row, a live status.
The server fills that placeholder by calling resources/read first, then dropping the returned text straight into the template.
This is the pattern that keeps a prompt accurate over time, since the fetch happens fresh at request time rather than baking stale facts into a fixed template.
7. Layering a System Instruction Over a User Template

blocks.alt: Layering a System Instruction Over a User Template
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697939-657975292.png
A user picks a prompt template by name and supplies arguments, but the server usually still wants to enforce its own baseline rules on top.
That baseline goes in first as a system message, and the filled user template goes in after, so the two never fight for the same slot.

items: The system instruction is written once by the server author and rarely changes.
The user template is chosen per request and filled with that request's arguments.
The composer places the system instruction first so the model treats it as the standing rule.
Nothing in the user template should be able to override the system instruction by accident.

blocks.text: This layering is what lets a server safely offer many different templates to choose from while keeping one guaranteed baseline behavior across all of them.
8. A Full Worked Composition
Here is a single function that combines all three pieces, a system instruction, a fetched resource, and a user selected template, into one message list.
Notice each piece stays a separate, named step. Anyone reading this function can tell exactly where each part of the final prompt came from.
9. Keeping Composed Prompts Readable
A composed prompt is only useful if a future maintainer can tell which piece produced which part of the final text.
Name each piece clearly, keep the composer function short, and avoid burying logic inside deeply nested string concatenation.
10. Naming and Organizing the Pieces
Give each reusable piece a name that describes its job, not its content, so it stays reusable across different final prompts.

blocks.text: 11. Avoiding the Tangled Mess
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697939-911195009.png
The tangled mess pattern usually starts small, one extra string concatenated in, then another, until nobody can say where a given sentence in the final prompt came from.
The fix is almost always the same, pull each concatenated piece back out into its own named function before it multiplies further.

blocks.title: A useful test
blocks.content: If you cannot point at one line and say exactly which piece produced it, the composition has already become a mess. Split it back apart.

blocks.text: 12. Order Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697940-999963968.png
The order pieces are placed in changes how a model weighs them. System instructions first, then any fetched facts, then the specific user ask, is a dependable default.
Putting facts after the instruction, rather than before it, helps the model treat the instruction as the standing rule and the facts as material to work with.
13. Handling a Missing or Failed Piece
Composition adds a new failure mode, one of the pieces might not be available, a resource fetch could fail, or an upstream prompt could return nothing useful.
A composer should check each piece before assembling the final prompt and fail clearly rather than silently sending the model a gap where content should have been.
A clear error at composition time is far easier to debug than a confusing model response caused by missing content nobody noticed.
14. Testing Composed Prompts
Because each piece is its own function, each piece can be tested on its own before ever checking the full composition.

items: Test the system instruction text stays stable across changes elsewhere.
Test the resource fetch and formatting separately from the template fill.
Test the full composed output only once the pieces are already trusted.

blocks.text: This layered testing catches most problems early, before they ever reach a real conversation with a user.
15. When Not to Compose
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440697940-641560518.png
A one off prompt used in exactly one place does not need to be split into reusable pieces, that would just add indirection for no benefit.
Reach for composition once you notice the same instruction, format, or fetch pattern showing up in more than one prompt.
Adding structure before there is a real second use case just adds indirection nobody benefits from yet.
16. Versioning Composed Prompts
Once a composed prompt is in real use, changing one of its pieces changes behavior for every caller, which makes casual edits riskier than they look.
Treat the composer function and its pieces like any other shared code, review changes, and keep a short changelog of what shifted and why.
Worked Example
Picture an MCP server that helps write pull request descriptions. It needs a system instruction, the diff content as a resource, and a user chosen template for tone.
Each part stays visible. If the description ever comes out wrong, a maintainer can check the system instruction, the diff fetch, or the template fill, one at a time.
Common Mistakes

items: Concatenating strings inline across many lines instead of naming each piece as its own function.
Letting the user supplied template override or contradict the system instruction.
Forgetting to check that a fetched resource actually returned content before composing.
Reusing one giant prompt for many purposes instead of composing smaller focused pieces.
Losing track of which piece produced which sentence once the prompt grows past a few lines.
Composing pieces in an order that buries the system instruction under a wall of fetched content.

blocks.text: Practice

Write a composer function for a prompt that drafts a meeting summary. It should combine a system instruction about staying neutral, a fetched transcript resource, and a user template for choosing a summary length.
Key Takeaway
Prompt composition means building a final prompt from small, named, reusable pieces, a system instruction, fetched resource content, and a user chosen template, instead of one hand written blob.
Keep each piece traceable and testable on its own, and the moment concatenation starts feeling tangled, that is the signal to split it back into clearly named functions.
